topic.title: Git & Version Control
topic.summary: How Git really works (three areas, commits as snapshots, the commit graph) and the everyday skills interviewers test: merge vs rebase, undoing changes, conflicts, fetch vs pull, stash, cherry-pick, branching strategies, pull requests and leaked secrets.
topic.overview:
## What interviewers expect

Every software team uses Git, so interviewers want proof that you can work in a shared repository without breaking it. Typical questions:

- **Fundamentals**: *What is the staging area?*, *What is a commit?*, *What is HEAD?*
- **Everyday operations**: *merge vs rebase*, *fetch vs pull*, *how do you undo a commit?*, *what is git stash?*
- **Teamwork**: *how do you resolve a merge conflict?*, *which branching strategy did your team use?*, *what makes a good pull request?*
- **Scenarios**: *you pushed a secret*, *you broke main*, *you lost a commit after a reset*.

## How to give a strong answer

1. Explain the **model** first: three areas, commits as snapshots with parent pointers, branches as pointers. Most commands become obvious once the model is clear.
2. Say what the command does to **history** (adds commits vs rewrites them) and whether that is safe on a **shared** branch.
3. Mention the **safety nets**: `git reflog`, `--force-with-lease`, `git merge --abort`, and "rotate the key first".

## How to study

Create a throwaway repository and try every command from this topic. Run `git log --oneline --graph --all` after each step and compare it with the gitGraph frames in the visuals. Break things on purpose (reset --hard, a conflicting merge, a rebase) and recover with `git reflog`.

cheatsheet.title: Model
points: Working tree → git add → index → git commit → local repo → git push → remote
Commit = snapshot (tree) + parent id(s) + author + message; id = SHA-1 of that content
Branch = movable pointer to a commit; HEAD = the branch you are on; tag = fixed pointer
origin/main = your local bookmark of the remote branch, updated by fetch

cheatsheet.title: Integrating
points: merge: merge commit with two parents, history preserved, safe on shared branches
rebase: replays commits as new ones (new ids), linear history; never on shared commits
fetch = download only; pull = fetch + merge (or --rebase / --ff-only)
Conflict: edit, remove markers, test, git add, git commit (or merge --continue / --abort)

cheatsheet.title: Undoing
points: git restore <file> discards edits; git restore --staged <file> unstages
git reset --soft / --mixed / --hard moves the branch back (local commits only)
git revert <id> = new inverse commit, the safe undo for pushed work
git reflog finds "lost" commits; push with --force-with-lease, never plain --force

cheatsheet.title: Team workflow
points: stash push -u -m to park work; stash pop to bring it back
cherry-pick -x to back-port a single fix to a release branch
GitHub Flow / trunk-based for continuous delivery; Git Flow for versioned releases
Small PRs with a description and green CI; leaked secret: rotate first, then filter-repo

git rebase origin/main          # fix conflicts: git add <file> && git rebase --continue
git push --force-with-lease     # only for your own branch

patterns.whenToUse: Choose by whether the commit is already shared.

git revert <id>                 # already pushed: add an inverse commit
git reflog                      # find anything you "lost"

questions.title: Working tree, staging area and repository: the basic Git workflow
questions.prompt:
Explain Git's **three areas** (working tree, staging area / index, repository) and how a change moves between them.

What do `git status`, `git add`, `git commit`, `git diff` and `git diff --staged` show, and where does `git push` fit in?
hints: A file you edit is not automatically part of the next commit. Which command decides what goes in?
Plain `git diff` compares two of the areas. Which two? And `--staged`?
Working tree → git add → index (the next commit’s exact content) → git commit → .git history → git push → remote. git diff = working tree vs index; git diff --staged = index vs last commit.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "You do git add, git commit, git push." The commands in order, but no idea what each area holds, so the candidate cannot explain why a file is missing from a commit or how to unstage it.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Names the three areas plus the remote, explains file states (untracked, modified, staged, committed), why staging exists (focused commits, git add -p), how each diff variant compares areas, the modern undo commands (git restore, git restore --staged), and that commits are local until pushed.

solution.summary: Git keeps three versions of your project: the **working tree** (the files you edit), the **staging area / index** (exactly what the next commit will contain) and the **repository** (the committed snapshots in `.git`). `git add` copies changes from the working tree into the index, `git commit` turns the index into a permanent commit, and `git push` uploads commits to a remote such as GitHub. Everything before the push is local.
solution.explanation:
### The areas
| Area | Where | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| **Working tree** | your project folder | the files as you see and edit them |
| **Staging area (index)** | `.git/index` | a snapshot of the **next** commit |
| **Local repository** | `.git/objects` + `.git/refs` | every commit, i.e. your history |
| **Remote** | GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket | the shared copy your team pushes to and fetches from |

### File states
- **Untracked**: a new file Git has never seen (`??` in `git status --short`).
- **Modified**: tracked, changed in the working tree but not staged (` M`).
- **Staged**: the change is in the index and will be in the next commit (`M `, or `A ` for a new file).
- **Committed / unmodified**: the working tree, the index and HEAD all agree.

### Why a staging area?
It lets you build commits **deliberately**. You fixed a bug and also reformatted three files? Stage and commit the fix alone, then the formatting, so each commit is small, reviewable and easy to revert. `git add -p` even stages individual *hunks* of a file.

### Which diff compares what
- `git diff`: working tree vs index (what you have **not** staged yet).
- `git diff --staged` (same as `--cached`): index vs HEAD (what **will** be committed).
- `git diff HEAD`: working tree vs the last commit (everything).

### Undoing at each level (Git 2.23+ commands)
- `git restore app.js`: throw away unstaged edits (copies the index version back over the file).
- `git restore --staged app.js`: unstage, but keep the edits in the working tree.
- `git commit --amend`: fix the last commit (only if it is not pushed yet).

### Remember
- `git commit` is **local**. Nobody sees it until you `git push`.
- Use a `.gitignore` for build output, `node_modules/`, IDE files and `.env` before your first `git add .`.

code.code:
git init -b main shop && cd shop
echo "console.log('hi');" > app.js
git status --short        # ?? app.js         untracked
git add app.js
git status --short        # A  app.js         staged (new file)
git commit -m "Add app entry point"

echo "// TODO: prices" >> app.js
git status --short        #  M app.js         modified, NOT staged
git diff                  # working tree vs index: + // TODO: prices
git add app.js
git diff                  # (empty) the index now matches the working tree
git diff --staged         # index vs HEAD: + // TODO: prices
git commit -m "Add TODO for prices"

git remote add origin git@github.com:rahim/shop.git
git push -u origin main   # only now do the commits leave your machine

keyPoints: Working tree → (git add) → index → (git commit) → local repository → (git push) → remote
The index is the exact snapshot of the next commit, which is why unstaged edits are not committed
git diff = working tree vs index; git diff --staged = index vs HEAD; git diff HEAD = working tree vs HEAD
git restore discards working-tree edits; git restore --staged unstages
Commits are local until pushed; use .gitignore before the first git add .

visuals.title: One change travelling through the areas
visuals.caption: Each panel is one area. v1, v2 are versions of a file’s content.

steps.note: You create `app.js`. It exists **only in the working tree**; Git calls it *untracked* (`?? app.js`).
`git add app.js` copies the current content (v1) into the **index**. This is now the snapshot of the next commit.
`git commit` stores the index as commit **C1** in the local repository. All three areas agree, so the tree is *clean*.
You edit the file again. Only the **working tree** changes (` M app.js`), and `git diff` shows the edit because it compares the working tree with the index.
You also create `notes.txt`, then `git add app.js` **only**. Now `git diff` is empty for app.js and `git diff --staged` shows v1 → v2. notes.txt stays untracked.
`git commit` records **only what was staged**: C2 contains app.js v2, and notes.txt is not part of it. This is how the staging area keeps commits focused.
Until now everything was **local**. `git push -u origin main` uploads C1 and C2 to GitHub and sets `origin/main` as the upstream for later pushes and pulls.

followUps.question: What does git add do internally?
followUps.answer: It writes the file content as a blob object into .git/objects (named by its SHA-1 hash) and records that blob’s hash for the path in the index. git commit later builds tree objects from the index and a commit object pointing to the top tree.

followUps.question: What is HEAD?
followUps.answer: A pointer to what you have checked out. Usually it points to a branch (the file .git/HEAD contains "ref: refs/heads/main"), and the branch points to its latest commit. In "detached HEAD" state it points straight at a commit.

followUps.question: What does git commit -a do?
followUps.answer: It automatically stages every modification and deletion of already tracked files before committing. It does not add untracked files, and it skips the chance to review what you are committing, so use it carefully.

questions.title: What is a Git commit? Snapshots, SHA-1 ids, parents and the DAG
questions.prompt:
What exactly does Git store when you run `git commit`?

Explain blob, tree and commit objects, how the commit id (hash) is computed, what parent pointers are, and why Git history is a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)**. What are branches and `HEAD` in this model?
hints: Does Git store the differences between versions, or whole snapshots?
If you change one character in the message of an old commit, what happens to its id, and to the id of every commit after it?

A commit = pointer to a tree (the snapshot) + parent id(s) + author/committer + message. Its id is the SHA-1 of exactly that text. Branches are movable pointers to commits; HEAD points at the current branch.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "A commit is a saved version of the code with a message." True but cannot explain why rebasing changes ids, why branches are cheap, or how Git detects corruption.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Describes the content-addressed object store (blob, tree, commit), how the id is a hash of the content including the parent ids, why that makes history immutable and tamper-evident, snapshots vs diffs (packfiles), parents and merges forming a DAG, and branches/HEAD/tags as plain refs.

solution.summary: A commit is an immutable object that records a full **snapshot** of the project (a tree of blobs), the id of its **parent** commit(s), the author, the committer and the message. Its id is the **SHA-1 hash of exactly that content**, so changing anything, including a parent, produces a different id. Because every commit points back to its parents, history forms a directed acyclic graph. A **branch** is just a movable pointer to one commit, and **HEAD** points to the branch you have checked out.
solution.explanation:
### The object store
`.git/objects` is a **content-addressed** key → value store. The key is the hash of the value.
- **blob**: the raw content of one file, with no name. id = SHA-1 of `"blob <size>\0<content>"`.
- **tree**: one directory listing: for each entry its mode, name and blob/tree id.
- **commit**: the id of the top tree, the parent id(s), author, committer, timestamps and message.
- (**annotated tag**: a named pointer to a commit that also stores the tagger, date, message and an optional signature.)

Identical content is stored **once**: if `README.md` did not change, the new tree simply points at the same blob again.

### Snapshots, not diffs
Conceptually every commit is a complete snapshot, which makes checkout, diff between any two commits, and branching fast. On disk, `git gc` packs objects into *packfiles* and delta-compresses them, so it is still space-efficient.

### The commit id
This is the real text that gets hashed for the second commit in the visual (prefixed by `commit <size>\0`):

```text
tree 850fb1395d7cd18a00cd7c58077528b519cc00b3
parent fd80f0609030474f11f801a482b16de6dd70eee7
author Rahim Uddin <rahim@example.com> 1767229200 +0600
committer Rahim Uddin <rahim@example.com> 1767229200 +0600

Bump app to v2
```

Change the message, the author, the timestamp, the snapshot **or the parent id**, and the hash changes. Consequences:
- History is **immutable** and **tamper-evident**: rewriting one old commit changes the id of every descendant.
- `commit --amend`, `rebase` and `cherry-pick` never edit commits; they create **new** ones with new ids.
- The default hash is SHA-1 (hardened against known collision attacks since Git 2.13). Repositories using SHA-256 are also supported.

### Parents and the DAG
- The first commit has **no parent**, a normal commit has **one**, a merge commit has **two** (or more).
- Arrows point from child to parent. A cycle is impossible, because a commit's id depends on its parents' ids, which must exist first.
- That is a **directed acyclic graph**. `git log --oneline --graph --all` draws it.

### Branches, HEAD and tags are just refs
- A **branch** is a file like `.git/refs/heads/main` that contains one commit id. Committing moves it forward. Creating a branch writes about 41 bytes, which is why branches are cheap.
- **HEAD** usually contains `ref: refs/heads/main`. In *detached HEAD* state it holds a commit id directly.
- A **tag** (`v1.4.0`) is a pointer that does not move.

### Explore it yourself
`git cat-file -p HEAD` (show the commit), `git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}` (its tree), `git hash-object file` (a blob id), `git rev-parse main` (where a branch points).

code.code:
printf '# Shop\n' > README.md
printf "console.log('shop v1');\n" > app.js
git hash-object README.md        # a00621bb3a9b990ee018f8d04c2d3140800d6ca6   (same content -> same id, on any machine)
git add . && git commit -m "Initial commit"
git cat-file -p HEAD             # tree 903a99514d2d7c6a879b52c9c787518b1530c9a8
                                 # author <name> <email> <unix time> <tz offset>   (no parent line)
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}      # 100644 blob a00621bb3a9b990ee018f8d04c2d3140800d6ca6    README.md
                                 # 100644 blob 3c2a9e4f6f5db4c2bf786627fdd465ae968d0d0f    app.js
cat .git/HEAD                    # ref: refs/heads/main
cat .git/refs/heads/main         # the id of the latest commit on main
git log --oneline --graph --all  # draw the DAG

keyPoints: Objects: blob (file content), tree (directory), commit (tree + parents + author + message)
The commit id is the SHA-1 of its content, so any change, including a parent, gives a new id
Git stores snapshots; packfiles delta-compress them on disk
Parent pointers make history a DAG: merge commits have two parents, cycles are impossible
Branches and tags are tiny refs to commits; HEAD points to the current branch

steps.note: `git add README.md app.js` stores each file’s content as a **blob**. The id is the hash of the content, so the same file always gets the same id, on every machine.
`git commit` writes a **tree** (names → blob ids) and a **commit** pointing at that tree, with no parent because it is the first commit. `main` now holds the commit id.
You change `app.js` and stage it: one **new blob** is written. README.md did not change, so its blob is **reused**, not copied.
The second commit gets a **new tree** (same README blob, new app.js blob) and records **parent fd80f06**. The `main` ref moves forward to it.

followUps.question: What is a detached HEAD, and how do you keep commits made there?
followUps.answer: HEAD points directly at a commit instead of a branch (after git checkout <id> or checking out a tag). New commits made there belong to no branch and become unreachable once you switch away. Create a branch first, e.g. git switch -c fix-from-tag.

followUps.question: How do you recover a commit you "lost" after a reset?
followUps.answer: git reflog lists every position HEAD and your branches have had (entries are kept for weeks by default). Find the id and run git branch rescue <id> or git reset --hard <id>.

followUps.question: Why can two people create the same blob id without talking to each other?
followUps.answer: Because the id is computed only from the content: the same bytes always give the same SHA-1. That is what lets Git deduplicate files and quickly decide which objects a remote already has.

questions.title: git merge vs git rebase
questions.prompt:
Your `feature` branch (commits C and D) is behind `main`, which got a new commit E. Compare bringing them together with `git merge` and with `git rebase`:

- what the history looks like afterwards,
- what happens to commit ids,
- how conflicts are handled,
- and when you must **not** rebase.
hints: Draw both results. Which one has a commit with two parents?
Rebase "moves" C and D onto E. Can Git really move an existing commit, given that its id depends on its parent?

Merge = a new merge commit, history preserved, safe for shared branches. Rebase = replay each commit on top of the target, producing new commits (C′, D′) and a linear history; never rebase commits others already have.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Rebase is cleaner, merge is messier." An opinion, without the mechanism or the risk of rewriting shared history.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Shows both resulting graphs, explains fast-forward vs three-way merges, that rebase replays patches and creates new ids, how conflicts differ (once vs per commit), the golden rule with force-with-lease, interactive rebase for clean-up, and typical team conventions (rebase locally, merge or squash via PRs).

solution.summary: `git merge` joins two histories with a new **merge commit** that has two parents. It preserves exactly what happened and is safe on shared branches. `git rebase` **replays** your commits one by one on top of the target branch, creating **new commits with new ids** and a linear history. Rebasing is great for tidying your own local branch, but never rebase commits that other people have already pulled.
solution.explanation:
### git merge
- **Fast-forward**: if `main` has no new commits since you branched, Git just moves the `main` pointer forward and creates no new commit. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit anyway (some teams want one per feature).
- **Three-way merge**: if both sides moved, Git compares each side with their **merge base** (the common ancestor) and creates a merge commit **M** with two parents.
- History is **true**: you can see when work was integrated. On busy repos it can look like a tangle of lines.
- Conflicts are resolved **once**, in the merge commit.

### git rebase
1. Find the merge base (B) of `feature` and `main`.
2. Save the changes each feature commit introduced (C, D).
3. Reset to the tip of `main` (E).
4. Re-apply the saved changes **one at a time**, creating **C′** and **D′** (same changes and messages, but a new parent, so new ids).
5. Move the `feature` ref to D′. The old C and D are left behind (reachable only through the reflog).

The result is a **linear** history, as if you had started your work today. Conflicts can appear **per replayed commit**: fix, `git add`, `git rebase --continue` (or `--abort`).

### The golden rule
**Do not rebase commits that exist outside your machine and that others may have built on.** Their copies still contain C and D while the server has C′ and D′, so you get duplicate commits and painful conflicts. If you rebase your *own* pushed feature branch, push with `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen.

### Interactive rebase
`git rebase -i HEAD~4` lets you **squash**, **fixup**, **reword**, **reorder** or **drop** commits before opening a pull request, turning "wip", "fix typo" and "really fix it" into one meaningful commit.

### What teams usually do
- Keep feature branches up to date with `git pull --rebase` or `git rebase origin/main` while they are private.
- Integrate into `main` through a pull request using **merge commit**, **squash merge** or **rebase-and-merge**: pick one convention.
- Never rewrite `main` or other shared branches.

code.code:
# Merge: integrate main into feature (or feature into main)
git switch feature
git merge main                    # creates merge commit M with parents D and E

# Rebase: replay feature's commits on top of the latest main
git switch feature
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main            # C, D are replayed as C', D' (new ids)
# conflict? edit the files, then:
git add price.js
git rebase --continue             # or: git rebase --abort to undo the whole rebase
git push --force-with-lease       # needed because feature's history was rewritten

# Tidy your own commits before a PR
git rebase -i HEAD~3              # pick / squash / fixup / reword / drop

# Only allow a fast-forward (no merge commit)
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feature

keyPoints: Merge = new merge commit with two parents; preserves history; safe on shared branches
Fast-forward merge just moves the pointer when the target has no new commits
Rebase replays commits as new commits (new ids) on top of the target, giving a linear history
Golden rule: never rebase commits others already have; use --force-with-lease for your own branch
Interactive rebase (squash/fixup/reword) cleans up local history before a PR

visuals.title: What git rebase main actually does
visuals.caption: ′ marks a replayed commit: same change and message, new parent, therefore a new id.

steps.note: Git finds the **merge base** of feature and main: commit B. The commits to replay are the ones on feature after B: C and D.
HEAD is detached at the tip of main (**E**). The changes of C and D are queued to be re-applied there.
Apply C’s change on top of E → **C′**. It has the same diff and message as C, but parent E instead of B, so it gets a **new id**.
Apply D → it touches lines E also changed: **CONFLICT**. The rebase pauses. You fix the file, run `git add`, then `git rebase --continue`.
D′ is created with your resolution. Conflicts are resolved **per replayed commit**, so a long branch can need several rounds.
Finally `feature` is moved to **D′** and HEAD re-attaches. The old C and D are unreachable (the reflog keeps them for a while). If feature was pushed, you now need `git push --force-with-lease`.

followUps.question: What is a fast-forward merge?
followUps.answer: If the target branch has no commits that your branch lacks, Git can just move the target pointer forward to your tip, so no merge commit is created. git merge --no-ff forces a merge commit; --ff-only refuses to merge unless a fast-forward is possible.

followUps.question: Squash merge vs rebase-and-merge in a PR?

followUps.question: Why is --force-with-lease safer than --force?
followUps.answer: It only overwrites the remote branch if it still points where your last fetch saw it. If a teammate pushed in the meantime, the push is rejected instead of silently deleting their commits.

questions.title: git reset vs git revert vs git restore
questions.prompt:
You need to undo something in Git. Explain the difference between:

- `git reset` with `--soft`, `--mixed` (the default) and `--hard`,
- `git revert`,
- `git restore` (and `git restore --staged`).

Which one is safe for a commit that is already pushed to a shared branch?
hints: Ask two questions for each command: does it move the branch pointer, and which areas (index, working tree) does it overwrite?
If teammates already pulled commit C3, what happens to them if C3 disappears from main?

restore = files only, history untouched. reset = move the branch back (--soft keeps changes staged, --mixed keeps them unstaged, --hard discards them); it rewrites history. revert = a new commit with the inverse change, safe for pushed work.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "reset deletes commits, revert undoes them." Vague, and does not say what happens to the working tree in each mode or which is safe after pushing.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains what each command does to HEAD/branch, index and working tree, gives the three reset modes precisely, shows revert as an inverse commit (and -m for merges), restore for files, the shared-history rule, and recovery with git reflog.

solution.summary: `git restore` discards or unstages changes in **files** without touching history. `git reset` moves the current **branch pointer** back to an earlier commit: `--soft` keeps the undone changes staged, `--mixed` (the default) keeps them in the working tree unstaged, and `--hard` throws them away. Reset rewrites history, so use it only on local commits. `git revert` creates a **new commit** that applies the inverse of an old one, which is the safe way to undo something that is already pushed.
solution.explanation:
### What each command touches
| Command | Moves branch / HEAD | Index | Working tree | Rewrites history |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `git reset --soft C2` | yes → C2 | unchanged (C3's changes stay staged) | unchanged | yes |
| `git reset --mixed C2` (default) | yes → C2 | reset to C2 | unchanged (changes become unstaged) | yes |
| `git reset --hard C2` | yes → C2 | reset to C2 | reset to C2 (**uncommitted work lost**) | yes |
| `git revert C3` | adds a new commit | updated | updated | **no** |
| `git restore file` | no | no | file reset to the index version | no |
| `git restore --staged file` | no | file reset to HEAD's version | no | no |

### When to use which
- **Unstage** a file you added by mistake: `git restore --staged file` (older: `git reset file`).
- **Throw away** local edits to a file: `git restore file` (older: `git checkout -- file`).
- **Redo the last local commit** (better message, add a file): `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, or simply `git commit --amend`.
- **Split or re-stage** the last local commits: `git reset HEAD~2` (mixed), then stage again in smaller pieces.
- **Abandon** local commits and edits completely: `git reset --hard origin/main`. Be careful: uncommitted work is unrecoverable.
- **Undo a pushed commit** on a shared branch: `git revert <id>`, then push. History stays intact, and everyone simply pulls the inverse commit.
- Reverting a **merge commit** needs a parent: `git revert -m 1 <merge-id>` keeps the first parent (main) as the mainline.

### Safety net
`reset` does not delete commits immediately; they just become unreachable. `git reflog` shows where HEAD was, and `git reset --hard <old-id>` brings them back (until garbage collection expires them, weeks later by default). Uncommitted changes destroyed by `--hard` or `restore` were never committed, so Git cannot recover them.

code.code:
git restore --staged secrets.env     # unstage, keep the file as it is
git restore app.js                   # discard unstaged edits in app.js

git reset --soft HEAD~1              # undo the last commit, keep its changes STAGED
git reset HEAD~1                     # (--mixed) undo it, keep the changes UNSTAGED
git reset --hard HEAD~1              # undo it AND discard the changes (local only!)

git revert 3f2a91c                   # new commit that inverts 3f2a91c: safe after push
git revert -m 1 9d0e4b2              # revert a merge commit, keeping parent 1 (main)
git push

git reflog                           # where HEAD has been: find a "lost" commit
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}            # go back to that position

keyPoints: restore works on files (working tree / index) and never touches history
reset moves the branch: --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstaged, --hard discards them
reset rewrites history: only for commits nobody else has
revert adds an inverse commit, which is the safe undo for pushed / shared commits (-m 1 for merges)
git reflog recovers commits after a bad reset; uncommitted work lost to --hard is gone

`git reset --mixed HEAD~1` (the default): the pointer moves **and** the index is reset to C2. The change survives only in the working tree, unstaged.
`git reset --hard HEAD~1`: pointer, index **and** working tree all go back to C2. C3 can still be found with `git reflog`, but uncommitted edits would have been lost for good.
`git revert C3` adds **C4**, which applies the inverse change (150 → 120). Nothing is rewritten, so this is the safe way to undo C3 if it was already pushed.

followUps.question: How do you undo the last commit but keep the changes?

questions.title: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
questions.prompt:
You run `git merge feature/discount` on `main` and Git prints:

```text
Auto-merging price.js
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in price.js
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

Explain why the conflict happened, what the conflict markers mean, and walk through resolving it safely. How can a team reduce conflicts?
hints: Git compares each branch with their common ancestor. When can it pick a side automatically, and when can it not?
Between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is one version; between `=======` and `>>>>>>>` is the other. Which is which?

Both branches changed the same lines since the merge base. Edit the file to the correct final code, delete the markers, run the tests, git add the file, then git commit (or git merge --continue). git merge --abort goes back.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Pick one version and delete the other." Risky: it silently drops a teammate’s change and never checks that the result works.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains three-way merging against the merge base, reads the markers (ours vs theirs, optional base with zdiff3), resolves by understanding both intents (talk to the author), removes markers, builds and tests, git add + commit / --continue, knows --abort, --ours/--theirs and that they swap during rebase, and lists prevention (small PRs, frequent integration, formatters).

solution.summary: A conflict happens when **both branches changed the same lines** (or one changed a file the other deleted) since their **common ancestor**, so Git’s three-way merge cannot choose automatically. Git writes both versions into the file between `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers. You edit the file to the correct final code, remove the markers, build and test, `git add` the file and finish with `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`). `git merge --abort` returns to the state before the merge.
solution.explanation:
### Why conflicts happen: the three-way merge
For every region of a file Git looks at three versions: the **base** (the merge base, i.e. the common ancestor), **ours** (the current branch, HEAD) and **theirs** (the branch being merged).
- Only one side changed the region → take that side automatically.
- Both sides made the **same** change → take it.
- Both sides changed it **differently** → **conflict**. Git does not guess.

Other conflict types: modify/delete (one side edited a file the other deleted), rename/rename, and binary files.

### Reading the markers
```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
  return price * 0.95;              ← ours: the branch you are on (main)
=======
  return Math.max(price - 50, 0);   ← theirs: the branch you are merging in
>>>>>>> feature/discount
```
With `git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3` Git also shows the **base** version between `|||||||` and `=======`, which makes it much easier to see what each side actually changed.

### Resolving safely
1. `git status` lists *Unmerged paths* (`both modified: price.js`).
2. Understand **both intents**: `git log --merge -p price.js`, the PR descriptions, or simply ask the other author. Often the right answer **combines** both changes.
3. Edit the file (or use the VS Code / IntelliJ merge editor, or `git mergetool`), then **delete every marker**.
4. **Build and run the tests**, because a textually clean merge can still be logically broken.
5. `git add price.js` marks it resolved, and `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`) creates the merge commit.
6. Changed your mind? `git merge --abort`.

Whole-file shortcuts: `git checkout --ours price.js` / `--theirs` (or `git restore --ours / --theirs`). During a **rebase** the meanings are swapped: *ours* is the branch you are rebasing onto, and *theirs* is your commit being replayed.

### Reducing conflicts in a team
- Small, short-lived branches and PRs; integrate with `main` often (daily).
- Auto-formatters and linters (Prettier, Spotless) so formatting never conflicts.
- Avoid giant shared files (one huge constants file, one routes file everybody edits), and split modules.
- Talk before big refactors; land them quickly.
- `git rerere` ("reuse recorded resolution") remembers how you resolved a conflict and re-applies it, which helps with long-running rebases.

code.code:
git switch main
git merge feature/discount
# Auto-merging price.js
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in price.js
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

git status                    # Unmerged paths: both modified: price.js
git diff                      # shows the conflicting hunk(s)
git log --merge -p price.js   # the commits on both sides that touched the file

# edit price.js -> keep the correct combined logic, delete all markers
npm test                      # never skip this
git add price.js              # mark as resolved
git commit                    # or: git merge --continue
# give up instead:  git merge --abort

git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3   # also show the base version

keyPoints: Conflict = both branches changed the same region differently since the merge base (three-way merge)
HEAD/ours = current branch (top section); theirs = branch being merged (bottom section)
Resolve by understanding both intents, remove all markers, build and test, then git add + commit
git merge --abort to back out; zdiff3 shows the base; ours/theirs swap during rebase
Prevent with small PRs, frequent integration and auto-formatting

followUps.answer: git log --merge -p <file> shows the commits from both sides that touched the conflicting file; git blame on each branch shows who changed the lines and why (then ask them).

followUps.question: What is a modify/delete conflict?
followUps.answer: One branch edited a file that the other deleted. Git cannot know whether the file should exist. Either keep it (git add file) with the edits, or confirm the deletion (git rm file), then commit.

followUps.question: How can you prevent the same conflict from recurring during a long rebase?
followUps.answer: Enable git rerere (git config rerere.enabled true). Git records how you resolved each conflict hunk and re-applies the same resolution automatically when it sees it again.

questions.title: git fetch vs git pull
questions.prompt:
What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`? What are remote-tracking branches such as `origin/main`?

Why do many developers prefer `git fetch` followed by a merge, or `git pull --rebase`, over a plain `git pull`?
hints: One of the two commands never changes your files or your branches. Which one?
Where does Git remember "what main looked like on GitHub the last time I checked"?
fetch = download commits and move origin/* refs only. pull = fetch + integrate origin/<branch> into your current branch (merge by default, or rebase / fast-forward-only if configured).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Pull gets the latest code, fetch also gets it." Does not say that fetch never touches your branch, or what pull does when histories diverged.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains remote-tracking branches, that fetch is always safe and lets you inspect before integrating, that pull = fetch + merge (or rebase / ff-only), the ahead/behind/diverged states, why --rebase avoids noisy merge commits, and useful config (pull.rebase, pull.ff, fetch --prune).

solution.summary: `git fetch` downloads new commits from the remote and updates **remote-tracking branches** like `origin/main`, but never touches your local branches or working tree. `git pull` is `git fetch` **plus** integrating `origin/<branch>` into your current branch: by merge by default, or by rebase with `--rebase`. Fetch is always safe; pull changes your branch.
solution.explanation:
### Remote-tracking branches
`origin/main` is your local, **read-only bookmark** of where `main` was on the remote the last time you talked to it. It only moves when you `fetch` (or `pull`, or `push`). Your own `main` is a separate branch that you move by committing, merging or rebasing.

### git fetch
- Downloads the missing objects and moves `origin/*` refs.
- **Never** changes your local branches, index or working tree, so it is safe to run any time.
- Afterwards you can inspect before integrating: `git log main..origin/main` (what is new on the remote), `git diff main origin/main`.
- `git status` then tells you if you are *behind*, *ahead* or have *diverged*.

### git pull
`git pull` = `git fetch` + integrate the upstream branch into the current branch:
- **Fast-forward** if you have no local commits: the branch pointer simply moves.
- **Merge** (the classic default) if both sides have commits: this creates a merge commit such as *"Merge branch 'main' of github.com:org/repo"*, which clutters history.
- **Rebase** with `git pull --rebase` (or `pull.rebase=true`): your local commits are replayed on top of `origin/main`, keeping history linear.
- **`--ff-only`**: refuse to do anything but a fast-forward.
- Recent Git versions refuse to pull diverged branches until you choose one of these strategies (`git config pull.rebase false|true` or `pull.ff only`).

### Good habits
- Fetch often. Pull (or rebase) before you start work and before you push.
- Prefer `git pull --rebase` for private feature branches; never rebase commits others already have.
- `git fetch --prune` deletes `origin/*` refs for branches that were deleted on the server.
- `git push` is rejected (*non-fast-forward*) if the remote moved since your last fetch: pull or rebase first, never "fix" it with `--force` on a shared branch.

code.code:
git fetch origin                     # download only: origin/main moves, your main does not
git status                           # Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 2 commits, and can be fast-forwarded.
git log --oneline main..origin/main  # what is new on the remote
git diff main origin/main            # what would change in your files
git merge origin/main                # integrate when you are ready (a fast-forward here)

git pull                             # = git fetch + git merge origin/main
git pull --rebase                    # = git fetch + git rebase origin/main (linear history)
git pull --ff-only                   # only if no merge commit is needed

git config --global pull.rebase true # make --rebase the default for git pull
git fetch --prune                    # also drop origin/* refs deleted on the server

keyPoints: origin/main is a local, read-only bookmark of the remote branch; it moves on fetch
fetch downloads and updates remote-tracking refs only, so it is always safe
pull = fetch + integrate (merge by default, or --rebase, or --ff-only)
Inspect after fetch with git log main..origin/main before integrating
pull --rebase avoids merge-commit noise on private branches; never rebase shared commits

followUps.answer: You have 3 local commits that the remote-tracking branch does not have, i.e. not pushed yet (as of your last fetch). git push will send them. "Behind" means the opposite; "diverged" means both.

followUps.question: What is an upstream branch?

followUps.question: Why was my push rejected with "non-fast-forward"?

questions.title: git stash and git cherry-pick
questions.prompt:
You are halfway through a feature when an urgent production bug arrives. How do you use `git stash` to switch context without committing half-finished work?

Later, the bug fix committed on `main` must also go to the `release/1.4` branch. How does `git cherry-pick` help, and what are its risks?
hints: You cannot switch branches safely with conflicting uncommitted changes. Where can they go temporarily?
Does `git stash` include new, untracked files by default?

stash push -u saves staged, unstaged and untracked changes on a stack and cleans the tree; stash pop re-applies and drops the entry. cherry-pick <id> applies the change of one commit as a NEW commit (new id) on the current branch, which is ideal for back-porting a fix.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Stash saves changes, cherry-pick copies a commit." Misses untracked files, pop vs apply, conflicts, and the duplicate-commit risk of cherry-picking.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Shows the full context-switch flow (stash push -u -m, switch, fix, switch back, pop), explains the stash as a stack (list, apply, drop, branch), how cherry-pick creates a new commit with -x for traceability, ranges, conflicts, and when to prefer merging forward instead.

solution.summary: `git stash` saves your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged, plus untracked files with `-u`) on a **stack** and cleans the working tree, so you can switch branches. `git stash pop` re-applies them later and drops the entry. `git cherry-pick <id>` takes the change introduced by one existing commit and applies it as a **new commit** on the current branch, which is how hotfixes are back-ported to release branches. The copy gets a new id and duplicates the change, so use it for targeted fixes, not to move whole branches.
solution.explanation:
### git stash
- `git stash push -m "WIP: payment form"` saves tracked changes (staged and unstaged) and resets the working tree to HEAD. Add `-u` (`--include-untracked`) for new files, which are **not** stashed by default.
- Stashes form a **stack**: `stash@{0}` is the newest. `git stash list` shows them, `git stash show -p stash@{1}` shows a diff.
- `git stash pop` = apply + drop. If applying causes a conflict, the entry is **kept** so nothing is lost.
- `git stash apply` applies but keeps the entry (useful to apply the same changes to several branches).
- `git stash branch wip-payment` creates a branch from the commit where you stashed and applies the stash there, which avoids conflicts when the branch has moved on.
- Under the hood a stash is a set of commits referenced by `refs/stash`.
- Alternatives: a "WIP" commit you amend later, or `git worktree add ../hotfix main` to have a second working directory.

### git cherry-pick
- `git cherry-pick 9fceb02` computes the diff between that commit and its parent and applies it on top of the current branch as a **new commit**: same message and author, but a **different id** (different parent).
- `-x` appends *"(cherry picked from commit 9fceb02…)"* to the message, which gives traceability across release branches.
- Ranges: `git cherry-pick A..B` (commits after A up to B); `-n` applies without committing.
- Conflicts work like a merge: fix, `git add`, `git cherry-pick --continue`, or `--abort`.

### Risks and good practice
- The same change now lives in two commits with different ids. Later merges usually cope, but can conflict if the code around it changed.
- Prefer **fix on the oldest supported branch, then merge forward** (release → main), as Git Flow does. Cherry-pick when that is not possible, or in trunk-based development (fix on main, cherry-pick into the release branch).
- Never use cherry-pick to "move" a whole feature; merge or rebase instead.

questions.title: Branching strategies: Git Flow vs GitHub Flow vs trunk-based development
questions.prompt:
Compare **Git Flow**, **GitHub Flow** and **trunk-based development**. How does each organise branches, releases and hotfixes?

Which would you choose for (a) a mobile banking app with releases every few weeks that must pass QA, and (b) a web SaaS product that deploys to production many times a day?
hints: Count the long-lived branches in each model. What does each extra branch cost?
What has to be true about tests and deployment if everyone merges to main several times a day?

Git Flow: main + develop + feature/release/hotfix branches, suited to versioned scheduled releases. GitHub Flow: one deployable main, short feature branches, PR, deploy. Trunk-based: tiny changes merged to main at least daily, unfinished work behind feature flags, release branches cut from trunk if needed.

approaches.name: Weak answer

approaches.name: Strong answer

solution.summary: **Git Flow** uses two long-lived branches (`main` and `develop`) plus feature, release and hotfix branches. It fits versioned, scheduled releases but adds a lot of process. **GitHub Flow** keeps one always-deployable `main`: a short-lived branch, a pull request, CI, merge, deploy. **Trunk-based development** goes further: everyone integrates small changes into `main` at least daily and hides unfinished work behind **feature flags**. That enables continuous delivery but needs strong automated tests.
solution.explanation:
### Git Flow
- **main**: production releases only, each one tagged (`v2.3.0`).
- **develop**: the integration branch for the next release.
- **feature/*** branches off develop and merges back into develop.
- **release/x.y**: cut from develop to stabilise (only fixes), then merged into **main** (and tagged) **and** back into develop.
- **hotfix/x.y.z**: cut from main for urgent production bugs, merged into main and develop.
- Pros: clear support for several versions and scheduled releases (mobile apps, on-premise software, banking releases that pass QA and approval).
- Cons: many long-lived branches, late integration, big merges, slow feedback. Even its author has noted it does not suit continuously delivered web apps.

### GitHub Flow
1. Branch off `main` (`feat/refund-button`).
2. Commit, push, open a **pull request**.
3. CI runs; teammates review.
4. Merge to `main` and **deploy right away** (main is always deployable).
- Simple, fast feedback, ideal for web services with continuous deployment.
- You need good CI, and some way to hide unfinished features if a branch cannot be finished quickly.

### Trunk-based development
- Everyone commits to **trunk** (`main`) directly or through **very short-lived** branches (hours, at most a day or two).
- Unfinished work is merged but switched off with **feature flags** (and branch-by-abstraction for big refactors).
- Releases are cut from trunk, with a **release branch** if you need to stabilise (for example an app-store build). Fixes go to trunk first and are cherry-picked into the release branch.
- Requires fast, reliable automated tests and code review that keeps up. This is what high-performing teams (per DORA research) tend to use.

### How to choose
- **Versioned, scheduled releases** with QA gates or several supported versions (mobile banking app, packaged software): Git Flow, or trunk-based with release branches.
- **Web/SaaS deploying many times a day**: GitHub Flow or trunk-based.
- Whatever you pick: protect `main` (required reviews and CI), keep branches short, tag releases (`vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, semantic versioning) and use clear names (`feature/PAY-142-bkash-refund`, `fix/…`, `hotfix/…`).
- Avoid "environment branches" (dev → qa → prod branches) that drift apart; promote the same build artifact through environments instead.

# ... commits, PR into develop ...

git switch main && git merge --no-ff release/2.3.0
git tag -a v2.3.0 -m "Release 2.3.0"
git switch develop && git merge --no-ff release/2.3.0
git switch -c hotfix/2.3.1 main              # urgent fix starts from production code

# GitHub Flow / trunk-based: short branch -> PR -> main -> deploy
git switch -c feat/refund-button main
git push -u origin feat/refund-button        # open a PR; CI + review; merge; deploy
# unfinished work ships dark behind a flag, e.g. if (flags.isOn("refund-button")) { ... }

GitHub Flow: one always-deployable main, short branches, PR + CI, deploy after merge
Trunk-based: merge small changes to main at least daily, feature flags hide unfinished work
Longer-lived branches = later integration = bigger merge conflicts and slower feedback
Choose by delivery style; always protect main, tag releases and keep branches short

followUps.question: What is a feature flag?
followUps.answer: A runtime switch (config, database or a service like LaunchDarkly/Unleash) that turns code paths on or off without deploying. It lets you merge unfinished work safely, release to a percentage of users, and roll back instantly. Remove old flags so they do not pile up.

followUps.question: What is semantic versioning?

questions.title: Pull requests and code review best practices
questions.prompt:
*"Walk me through how a change gets merged in your team."*

Explain what makes a good pull request (size, title and description, commits, tests), how you review someone else’s PR, and how you handle review comments on your own.
hints: Would you rather review 200 lines or 2,000? Which review finds more bugs?
What does a reviewer need to know before reading the diff?

Small focused PR + clear description (what, why, how to test, screenshots, ticket) + green CI. Review for correctness, tests, security and design first; automate style. Comment specifically and kindly, reply to every comment, merge only after approval and passing checks.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "I push my code and someone approves it." No sense of PR size, description, CI, review focus or how to respond to feedback.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Describes the full lifecycle (branch → small commits → self-review → PR with template → CI → review → address comments → merge strategy → delete branch → monitor), with concrete reviewer priorities, comment etiquette (nit:, questions, suggestions), and how to disagree constructively.

solution.summary: A good PR is **small and focused** (ideally a few hundred lines), has a clear **title and description** (what, why, how to test, screenshots, linked ticket), passes **CI**, and has clean commits. Reviewers look at **correctness, tests, security and design first** and leave style to automated tools, writing specific, kind, actionable comments. As the author you self-review first, respond to every comment, push fixes, and merge only after approval and green checks.
solution.explanation:
### As the author
1. **One purpose per PR.** Split refactoring from behaviour changes. Small PRs get faster and better reviews.
2. **Self-review the diff first**: remove debug logs and commented-out code, check naming, add tests.
3. **Meaningful commits** in the imperative mood: `fix(auth): refresh token before expiry` ([Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org) style is common).
4. **Description**: what changed, *why*, how to test it, screenshots for UI changes, risks and rollout (feature flag, migration), and a link to the ticket (`PAY-142`).
5. Make **CI green** (build, tests, lint, security scan) before asking for review. Draft PRs are fine for early feedback.
6. **Respond to every comment**: fix it, or explain why not. Push follow-up commits so reviewers can see what changed, and resolve threads.

### As the reviewer
1. Understand the **goal** first: read the description and the ticket.
2. **Correctness**: edge cases, null and empty inputs, error handling, concurrency, transactions.
3. **Tests**: do they cover the change and its failure paths?
4. **Security**: input validation, authorization checks, secrets, SQL injection, logging of personal data.
5. **Design and readability**: the right layer, naming, duplication, simpler alternatives.
6. **Style last**: formatters and linters should make most style comments unnecessary.
7. Comment on the **code, not the person**; ask questions (*"What happens if `items` is empty?"*), label optional points (`nit:`), suggest concrete code, and approve when it is good enough rather than perfect.
8. Review **promptly** (within a working day), because waiting PRs block teammates.

### Merging
- Strategies: **merge commit** (keeps every commit), **squash merge** (one clean commit per PR), **rebase and merge** (linear, keeps commits). Teams pick one.
- Branch protection: required approvals, required checks, CODEOWNERS.
- After merging: delete the branch, watch the deployment and the metrics, and close the ticket.

### Handling disagreement
Move long threads to a quick call, decide based on team conventions or data, and write the outcome in the PR. If it is a matter of taste, the author decides.

questions.title: You committed and pushed a secret (API key, .env). What now?
questions.prompt:
You accidentally committed a `.env` file containing a live payment API key and pushed it to GitHub.

What do you do, **in order**? How do you remove the key from Git history, why is deleting the file in a new commit not enough, and how do you prevent this from happening again?
hints: Assume someone has already copied the key. What is the only action that makes the leaked key useless?
After `git rm .env && git commit`, can someone still see the key? Try `git show <old-commit>:.env`.

Rotate/revoke first. Then remove it from code (env vars / secret manager, .gitignore). If it was pushed, rewrite history (git filter-repo or BFG), force-push, have everyone re-clone, and contact the host to purge cached refs. Prevent with .gitignore, pre-commit secret scanning and push protection.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Delete the file and commit again" (or git revert). The key stays in history forever and is still valid.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Rotates the key immediately, explains that history keeps every version, distinguishes unpushed (amend / interactive rebase) from pushed (filter-repo + force push + re-clone + host cleanup), notes that all later commit ids change, and adds prevention: .gitignore, secret managers, pre-commit hooks (gitleaks), GitHub secret scanning and push protection.

solution.summary: First treat the secret as **compromised**: revoke or rotate it immediately, because bots scan public pushes within minutes and anyone with a clone already has it. Then move it out of the code (environment variables or a secret manager, plus `.gitignore`). If it was pushed, **rewrite history** with `git filter-repo` (or BFG), force-push, have collaborators re-clone, and ask the host to purge cached references. A delete commit or `git revert` does **not** remove it from history. Prevent recurrence with pre-commit secret scanning and push protection.
solution.explanation:
### 1. Rotate first, always
History rewriting takes time and cannot reach copies that already exist (forks, clones, CI caches, scrapers). The only real fix is to make the leaked value **useless**: revoke the key in the provider's console (AWS, Stripe, bKash, database password), issue a new one, and check the provider's logs for misuse.

### 2. Why "delete and commit" is not enough
Git keeps every snapshot. After `git rm .env && git commit`, anyone can still run `git log --all -- .env` and `git show <old-id>:.env`. `git revert` also only adds a new commit. The secret is still in the history.

### 3. Remove it from history
**Not pushed yet** (the easy case):
- It is in the last commit: `git rm --cached .env`, add it to `.gitignore`, `git commit --amend`.
- It is in an older local commit: `git rebase -i <commit>^`, mark the commit as `edit`, remove the file, amend, `git rebase --continue`.

**Already pushed**:
- Use **git filter-repo** (the tool recommended by the Git project; BFG Repo-Cleaner is an older alternative) on a fresh clone:
  - `git filter-repo --invert-paths --path .env` removes the file from every commit,
  - or `git filter-repo --replace-text secrets.txt` keeps the file but replaces the secret value everywhere.
- Every commit from the first bad one onwards gets a **new id**. Force-push all branches and tags, then everyone must **re-clone** (or hard-reset); an old clone pushed back would re-introduce the secret.
- On GitHub, cached views and pull-request refs can still show the old commits; contact GitHub Support to purge them. Forks are separate copies.

### 4. Fix the code
Read secrets from environment variables or a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GitHub Actions secrets), commit a `.env.example` with placeholders, and add `.env` to `.gitignore`. Note that `.gitignore` does not untrack files that are already tracked; `git rm --cached` does.

### 5. Prevent it next time
- **Pre-commit hooks** with secret scanners (gitleaks, git-secrets, detect-secrets) block the commit locally.
- **GitHub secret scanning and push protection** reject pushes that contain known key formats.
- Review diffs before committing (`git diff --staged`), and never use `git add .` in a folder without a `.gitignore`.

code.code:
# 0. FIRST: revoke / rotate the key in the provider's console. Check its access logs.

# 1. Not pushed yet: fix the local commit
git rm --cached .env                       # stop tracking it, keep the file on disk
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit --amend --no-edit               # older commit? use: git rebase -i <bad-commit>^

# 2. Already pushed: rewrite history with git-filter-repo (in a fresh clone)
git clone git@github.com:acme/shop.git shop-clean && cd shop-clean
git filter-repo --invert-paths --path .env           # drop .env from every commit
# or keep the file but scrub the value:
#   git filter-repo --replace-text ../secrets.txt     # line format: sk_live_51H8xyz==>***REMOVED***
git remote add origin git@github.com:acme/shop.git   # filter-repo removes 'origin' as a safety net
git push origin --force --all
git push origin --force --tags

# 3. Everyone re-clones; ask GitHub Support to purge cached views / PR refs if needed.

# Prevention: scan before every commit
gitleaks git --pre-commit --staged        # e.g. from a pre-commit hook (gitleaks < 8.19: gitleaks protect --staged)

followUps.question: Why is git filter-repo preferred over git filter-branch?
followUps.answer: filter-branch is very slow and easy to misuse; the Git documentation itself recommends git filter-repo instead. filter-repo is much faster, has safer defaults (it insists on a fresh clone) and has simple options like --path, --invert-paths and --replace-text.

followUps.question: How should a Spring Boot or Node app read secrets?
followUps.answer: From the environment or a secret manager, never from committed files: ${DB_PASSWORD} placeholders in application.yml or process.env.DB_PASSWORD in Node, injected by Docker/Kubernetes secrets, Vault or AWS Secrets Manager. Commit a .env.example with dummy values for documentation.

followUps.question: The repository is private. Do you still need to rotate?
followUps.answer: Yes. Everyone with access (current and former members, CI systems, third-party integrations, laptops that get stolen) has the key, and private repositories can become public or leak later. Rotation is cheap compared with a breach.

quiz.question: Given this output, which file(s) will be in the commit if you now run `git commit -m "..."` (without -a)?

code.code:
$ git status --short
M  app.js
 M README.md
?? notes.txt

options: app.js, README.md and notes.txt
Only app.js
app.js and README.md
Nothing, because notes.txt is untracked
quiz.explanation: The first column is the index. "M " means app.js is staged; " M" means README.md is modified but NOT staged; "??" means notes.txt is untracked. A commit records only the index, so only app.js goes in.

quiz.question: Which of these does NOT change the id (hash) of an existing commit?
options: Editing its message with git commit --amend
Rebasing it onto a different parent
Changing its author date
Creating a new branch that points to it
quiz.explanation: A commit id is the hash of its tree, parent ids, author/committer (with dates) and message, so the first three all produce a new commit with a new id. A branch is just a separate pointer to the commit; creating one does not touch the commit.

quiz.question: You run `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. Where are the changes from the undone commit?
options: Staged in the index, ready to commit again
Unstaged in the working tree only
Deleted permanently
Moved to the stash
quiz.explanation: --soft only moves the branch pointer, leaving both the index and the working tree untouched, so the changes show up as staged. --mixed (the default) would leave them unstaged; --hard would discard them.

quiz.question: A bad commit is already pushed to the shared main branch and teammates have pulled it. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~1 && git push --force
git commit --amend
git revert <commit> and push
git restore .
quiz.explanation: git revert adds a new commit that applies the inverse change, so history is not rewritten and everyone can simply pull it. reset + force push rewrites shared history; amend rewrites the latest commit; restore only touches files.

quiz.question: You rebase your feature branch (commits C and D) onto the latest main. What is true afterwards?
options: C and D keep their ids but get a new parent
C and D are replaced by new commits C′ and D′ with new ids
A merge commit with two parents is created
main now contains C and D
quiz.explanation: A commit’s id depends on its parent, so Git cannot move commits. Rebase replays their changes as new commits on top of main. No merge commit is created, and main itself does not move until you merge or fast-forward it.

quiz.question: On main you ran `git merge feature`, which conflicted. In the file below, what is between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======`?

code.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
  return price * 0.95;
=======
  return Math.max(price - 50, 0);
>>>>>>> feature

options: The version from main (the branch you are on)
The version from feature
The common ancestor (base) version
The final merged result
quiz.explanation: HEAD is the current branch, main ("ours"). The part after ======= comes from the branch being merged ("theirs"). The base is only shown with the diff3/zdiff3 conflict style, between ||||||| and =======.

quiz.question: What does `git fetch origin` change?
options: Your local main branch and your working tree
Only your working tree
Nothing at all until you run git pull
Only the remote-tracking branches such as origin/main (plus downloaded objects)
quiz.explanation: fetch downloads new commits and moves origin/* refs. Your local branches, index and files are untouched. git pull = fetch + merge (or rebase) into your current branch.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `git stash pop` and `git stash apply`?
options: pop includes untracked files, apply does not
apply re-applies the stash and keeps the entry; pop re-applies it and drops the entry (unless there is a conflict)
pop applies the oldest stash, apply the newest
There is no difference
quiz.explanation: Both re-apply stashed changes (newest by default). pop also removes the entry from the stash stack, but keeps it if applying caused a conflict. Untracked files depend on whether they were stashed with -u, not on pop vs apply.

quiz.question: You run `git cherry-pick 9fceb02` on release/1.4. What happens?
options: release/1.4 is merged with the branch that contains 9fceb02
Commit 9fceb02 is moved from its branch to release/1.4
The change introduced by 9fceb02 is applied as a new commit with a new id on release/1.4
All commits up to 9fceb02 are copied to release/1.4
quiz.explanation: cherry-pick takes the diff between that commit and its parent and commits it on the current branch. The original stays where it was; the copy has a different parent and therefore a different id. Use -x to record the source id.

quiz.question: Which workflow keeps one always-deployable main branch, uses short-lived feature branches merged through pull requests, and deploys after each merge?
options: GitHub Flow
Git Flow
Forking workflow with a develop branch
Release-train model with environment branches
quiz.explanation: That is GitHub Flow. Git Flow adds a long-lived develop branch plus release and hotfix branches; trunk-based development goes even further with very short branches and feature flags.

quiz.question: Which pull request is most likely to get a fast, high-quality review?
options: A 3,000-line PR titled "changes" that also reformats the whole project
A PR opened with a failing CI build and the note "will fix tests later"
A PR with no description, because the code is self-explanatory
A 250-line PR doing one thing, with a description, test steps and green CI
quiz.explanation: Small, single-purpose PRs with context (what, why, how to test) and passing checks let reviewers focus on correctness and design. Huge mixed diffs get skimmed, and red builds waste reviewers’ time.

quiz.question: You just pushed a live payment API key to a public repository. What should you do FIRST?
options: Run git revert on the commit
Delete the file and push a new commit
Revoke / rotate the key with the provider
Make the repository private
quiz.explanation: Assume the key is already compromised: bots scan public pushes within minutes. Rotating it is the only action that makes the leaked value useless. Then clean the history (filter-repo + force push) and add prevention. A revert or delete commit leaves the key in history.
